source.title: AlphaSteer: Learning Refusal Steering with Principled Null-Space Constraint
source.authors: Leheng Sheng; Changshuo Shen; Weixiang Zhao; Jun-Feng Fang; Xiao-Hao Liu; Zhen-Kai Liang; Xiang Wang; An Zhang; Tat-Seng Chua

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study extracts a refusal vector using a difference in mean activations and directly adds that vector to model activations, then measures refusal on jailbreak prompts and performance on benign utility benchmarks. It does not reproduce the ablation part of V1.
record.gate_note: The paper also evaluates AlphaSteer, a learned prompt-dependent transformation, but those results are not treated as tests of the single-vector claim. The single-vector results used here are the direct refusal-vector (RV) ablation baseline. The paper reports per-attack DSR values, but the flattened table layout does not reliably associate all individual cells with RV; the reported aggregate DSR values are retained. Values used to select layers and steering settings are not recorded as outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study builds a difference-in-means refusal vector (RV) and adds it at selected middle layers of three instruct models as an ablation baseline. It reports how often refusal is induced on jailbreak prompts and on harmless prompts. That bears on V1's addition component in a jailbreak-defence setting. It is not T1: there is no directional ablation, no every-layer projection, and the contrast sets differ. The vector is refused-minus-complied malicious prompts (Appendix D.1), not harmful-minus-harmless instructions.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude AlphaSteer raises jailbreak refusal while keeping utility near the vanilla model. Applying the refusal vector directly reaches about 100% DSR but very low utility scores, which they read as the safety–utility trade-off of indiscriminate steering. They do not frame this as evidence about the single-direction mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a difference-in-means refusal vector and activation addition, but evaluates the direct-vector ablation on selected middle layers rather than testing removal at every layer and position; the paper's principal method is a learned prompt-dependent transformation.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper selects steering layers based on separation of steering-vector norms and reports different steering strengths by model. In the direct RV benchmark, utility outcomes vary across models and benchmarks. The adaptive-GCG result is a separate attack condition.
record.problems: The reported DSR and utility evaluations use automated judges, with GPT-4o used for the main DSR evaluation. No error bars or other uncertainty estimates are reported. The tested direct-vector intervention is limited to selected middle layers, and the per-attack cells in the flattened Table 1 cannot be reliably assigned to RV from the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Individual attack-specific RV DSR cells from Table 1 were not extracted because the flattened layout does not reliably associate every value with its method and attack column. Aggregate DSR rows from Table 1 are included instead. Other methods' results and AlphaSteer's results were not included as rows because they do not measure the direct single-vector intervention.

untested.parts: Directional ablation (projecting the direction out) to remove refusal is not tested. Whether other abilities are kept under ablation is not tested. The vector contrasts refused vs complied malicious prompts rather than harmful vs harmless instructions, and is added only at selected middle layers.

missing.what: RV DSR judged by Llama-Guard-3-8B (100% on every attack, Llama-3.1-8B), a judge-robustness check for r1
Per-attack RV DSR cells: all 100 except Gemma PAIR 96. They are readable from the Table 1 rows and could replace the aggregates.
RV performance vs steering strength sweep (DSR and utility); figure only, no numbers in text

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label is not supported. V1 predicts that adding the direction induces refusal everywhere, including on harmless prompts. The XSTest drops therefore confirm the addition component, and the math and AlpacaEval drops cannot be separated from induced refusals. The case studies show some RV outputs are degenerate (e.g., garbled Llama output on a Base64 prompt), but this is qualitative. The RV vector here is refused-minus-complied over malicious prompts at the last token, a variant of the original contrast. The tranche is T3 (jailbreak-defence setting), not T1.

versions.untested_parts: The study adds the difference-in-means refusal vector at selected middle layers; it does not project the vector out of every layer and position or test whether that removal eliminates refusal.
No weight edit or abliteration of released model weights is tested.
The adaptive GCG evaluation measures refusal after attack, but does not test whether attacks work by suppressing the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
The study does not compare a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account of refusal.
The study does not separate harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Models are evaluated with vectors derived for their own activations; the study does not test cross-language transfer or transfer of a vector between model variants, or from base to instruct models.
The paper compares its steering method with refusal fine-tuning, but does not test whether training choices determine the existence of a removable refusal direction.
The limitations section says effectiveness on large reasoning models is unknown.

rows.locator: Appendix E.6, Figure 7 and accompanying text

rows.check: Under an adaptive white-box GCG attack, RV addition raises DSR only from 57.5% to 79.5%, versus 100% for non-adaptive attacks. The location is Figure 7 (an inline table) in Appendix E.6, Llama only.

relationships.condition: RV addition on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma-2-9b, non-adaptive jailbreak attacks and harmless XSTest prompts (Llama, Gemma)
relationships.reason: Adding RV raises average DSR to 100/100/99.37% from 48/20.6/24.7% (r1–r3). It also induces refusal on safe prompts, cutting compliance to 4.0% and 6.0% (r4, r14).
relationships.display_finding: Defense success rose from 48%, 20.6% and 24.7% to 100%, 100% and 99.37% in Llama, Qwen and Gemma respectively, while safe-prompt compliance fell to 4.0% in Llama and 6.0% in Gemma.

Caveats: the direction contrasts refused vs complied malicious prompts, not harmful vs harmless. DSR counts any non-assisting output: Fig. 21 shows Llama+RV giving garbled base64 text.

relationships.condition: Qwen2.5-7B on harmless XSTest prompts; Llama-3.1-8B under adaptive white-box GCG

relation.reason: The study's own Tables 1–2 and App. E.6 report refusal and defence rates from adding the refusal vector on three models. That bears on V1's addition component.

tranche.reason: This is a jailbreak-defence paper that reports the effect of adding the direction on its own (the RV ablation baseline), so it is not T4. It is not T1. The RV is a difference-in-means between refused and complied malicious prompts (App. D.1), not harmful minus harmless. Only addition is tested, judged by GPT-4o DSR/CR. The record's recipe note does not mention the different contrast set.

source_check.notes: The RV is built per layer from last-token activations on 720 malicious prompts, split by whether the model refused or complied (App. D.1). It is not V1's harmful-minus-harmless contrast. Only addition is tested; directional ablation is not. The paper doesn't state RV's steering strength or layers apart from AlphaSteer's middle layers. Quoted jailbreak prompts in the case studies are attack examples, not instructions.

statements.correction: Table 2, RV utility (AlpacaEval/MATH/GSM8K): Llama 10.4/37.0/65.0 (vanilla 50.0/45.0/81.0); Qwen 4.5/2.0/1.0 (vanilla 50.0/67.0/96.0); Gemma 3.5/0.0/0.0 (vanilla 50.0/44.0/79.0). These scores are not split into refusals and capability loss.
statements.problem: None for this study. RV is applied to all prompts (Sec. 1, Table 2), so drops on AlpacaEval, MATH and GSM8K can't be separated from induced refusals. The paper never separates them. The statement names only r5–r8 (presumably Llama). Table 2 also reports RV utility for Qwen and Gemma, which would have the same problem.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Direct RV steering on the tested jailbreak attack sets
reader_labels.reason: Adding RV yields reported aggregate DSR of 100.00%, 100.00%, and 99.37% for the three models (r1–r3), supporting the refusal-induction component.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Direct RV steering on tested harmless utility benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: Harmless-prompt compliance and general utility fall substantially, including near-zero math accuracy for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9b-IT (r4–r18), contrary to the claim that other abilities remain largely intact.
